contract.note: The contract scores the predicted outcome and ignores the doubt framing. Under policy, graded or probabilistic language is not scored. It also leaves 'great' and 'resolved errors' undefined.

contract.note: The contract treats the improbability judgment as a scorable directional forecast, but policy excludes probabilistic language. 'Fundamentally new' also has no threshold, so the result would turn on the evaluator's view of novelty.

reviews.rationale: 'It would be astounding' expresses very low probability rather than a firm commitment, so policy says it is not scored. Even if it were scored, the packet cannot settle whether ASI-Arch or any other work crossed the 'fundamentally new' bar, so it would be unresolved.

contract.note: The plain reading, limited practical progress toward reliable safety and control with some results allowed, is ordinary and fair. 'Little' has no threshold, so interpretation still matters.

evidence.note: Broad Jan 2025 review: progress, but methods are 'fundamentally limited'. No method reliably prevents overtly unsafe actions, and jailbreaks take low to moderate effort. This matches fragile gains.
Independent 2024 study: nearly 100% jailbreak success on leading safety-aligned models, showing fragile safeguards. Earlier model generation.
OpenAI's own Dec 2024 paper reports large jailbreak-robustness gains for o1. It is a single company benchmark, not broad durable control.

reviews.rationale: The support condition allows gains that are small, narrow or fragile. The broad review (e4) and the independent attack study (e5) show alignment gains up to May 2025 stayed fragile and fundamentally limited. e6 shows real gains, but it is one company benchmark, which the contract says cannot establish broad, durable improvement.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own Substack post.

semantics.note: Captures the deployment count, the denominator and the 2012 promise. 'We would all have' is a loose rhetorical paraphrase of an unnamed promise.

contract.note: Defining service as ordinary riders with no safety driver is a fair plain reading. Requiring the 2012 promise to mean literal universal access reads a rhetorical paraphrase strictly, so that part should not decide the result.

evidence.note: Waymo's own May 2025 post lists 4 US service markets. It is a partial inventory, and metro markets are not municipalities.
Baidu's own May 2025 earnings call says its 'footprint' spans 15 cities. It does not show fully driverless public service in each one.
Sept 2012 report: Brin said ordinary people could 'experience' self-driving within about 5 years. That is softer than everyone having one, and may not be the promise Marcus meant.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no deduplicated worldwide list of fully driverless public services in May 2025. Waymo's 4 markets plus an unclear Baidu footprint cannot confirm or refute 'about 10'. The 20,000-city denominator has no source, and the 2012 promise cannot be pinned down. The evidence does not settle the claim.
